questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: Match the six histological layers of the human cerebral neocortex (from superficial pial surface to deep white matter) with their primary input/output roles:
options: I: molecular; II: external granular; III: external pyramidal; IV: internal granular (thalamic input); V: internal pyramidal (descending output); VI: multiform (thalamic feedback)
I: molecular; II: external granular; III: internal granular (thalamic input); IV: external pyramidal; V: multiform; VI: internal pyramidal (descending output)
I: molecular; II: external pyramidal; III: external granular; IV: internal pyramidal (descending output); V: internal granular (thalamic input); VI: multiform
I: molecular; II: internal granular; III: external pyramidal; IV: multiform; V: external granular; VI: internal pyramidal
questions.explain: Mnemonic: Layer IV = 'In' (thalamic sensory input; prominent in striate visual cortex V1/Brodmann 17), Layer V = 'Ventricle/Spinal exit' (corticospinal/corticobulbar motor output; prominent in precentral M1/Brodmann 4), Layer VI = 'Thalamus feedback.' The six layers are, from superficial to deep: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal and multiform. Layer IV receives specific thalamocortical sensory input; layer V sends corticobulbar/corticospinal output (including Betz cells); layer VI provides corticothalamic feedback.

open.q: State the primary projection function of cortical Layer IV, Layer V, and Layer VI in the six-layered cerebral neocortex.
accept: Layer IV (internal granular): receives specific thalamocortical sensory afferents; Layer V (internal pyramidal): sends descending motor projections to brainstem and spinal cord (corticobulbar/corticospinal); Layer VI (multiform): sends corticothalamic feedback projections
Thalamic sensory input (Layer IV), brainstem/spinal motor output (Layer V), corticothalamic feedback (Layer VI)

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: Match the key Brodmann cortical areas with their anatomical gyri and primary physiological functions:
options: 4: precentral/motor; 3,1,2: postcentral/sensory; 17: calcarine/visual; 41,42: Heschl/auditory; 44,45: inferior frontal/Broca; 22: posterior superior temporal/Wernicke
4: postcentral/sensory; 3,1,2: precentral/motor; 17: Heschl/auditory; 41,42: calcarine/visual; 44,45: posterior temporal/Wernicke; 22: inferior frontal/Broca
4: precentral/motor; 3,1,2: calcarine/visual; 17: postcentral/sensory; 41,42: inferior frontal/Broca; 44,45: Heschl/auditory; 22: posterior temporal/Wernicke
4: inferior frontal/Broca; 3,1,2: postcentral/sensory; 17: calcarine/visual; 41,42: Heschl/auditory; 44,45: precentral/motor; 22: posterior temporal/Wernicke
questions.explain: Brodmann's cytoarchitectural map links cortical microanatomy directly to sensory, motor, and associative localization. Area 4 is in the precentral gyrus; areas 3, 1 and 2 are in the postcentral gyrus; area 17 surrounds the calcarine sulcus; areas 41 and 42 are in Heschl's transverse temporal gyri; areas 44 and 45 are in the inferior frontal gyrus; area 22 is in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

open.q: Identify the Brodmann area numbers and cortical lobes for: (1) primary motor cortex, (2) primary somatosensory cortex, (3) primary visual cortex, and (4) primary auditory cortex.
accept: 1) Primary motor: Area 4 (frontal lobe); 2) Primary somatosensory: Areas 3, 1, 2 (parietal lobe); 3) Primary visual: Area 17 (occipital lobe); 4) Primary auditory: Areas 41, 42 (temporal lobe)

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: How is the body represented in the 'motor and sensory homunculi' along the precentral and postcentral gyri, and which cerebral arteries supply each region?
options: Contralateral inverted map; face/arm lateral (MCA), leg/perineum medial (ACA)
Ipsilateral upright map; face/arm medial (ACA), leg/perineum lateral (MCA)
Contralateral inverted map; face/arm medial (ACA), leg/perineum lateral (MCA)
Ipsilateral inverted map; all body regions supplied by the PCA
questions.explain: Cortical magnification reflects innervation density and motor precision (fingers/speech), while ACA vs MCA vascular territory explains why ACA strokes cause contralateral leg weakness and MCA strokes cause contralateral face/arm weakness. The homunculus is contralateral and inverted, with cortical magnification of the hand, lips and tongue. The lateral convexity represents the face and upper limb (MCA territory); the medial paracentral lobule represents the lower limb and perineum (ACA territory).

open.q: Which cerebral artery supplies the lower-limb region versus the face/upper-limb region of the primary motor and somatosensory homunculi?
accept: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) supplies the medial paracentral lobule (lower limb/perineum); Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) supplies the lateral convexity (face, upper limb, trunk)
ACA (lower limb) vs MCA (face and upper limb)

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: What are the functional specializations of the 'categorical (left in ~95% of right-handers and ~70% of left-handers)' versus 'representational (right, visuospatial)' cerebral hemispheres?
options: Left: language and analytical/sequential processing; right: visuospatial processing, face recognition and emotional prosody
Left: visuospatial processing and face recognition; right: language and mathematical calculation
Left: primary vision and hearing; right: primary motor control and language
Both hemispheres specialise identically; the corpus callosum prevents functional lateralisation
questions.explain: Split-brain (callosotomy) studies by Roger Sperry demonstrated that objects shown solely to the left visual field (processed by the right hemisphere) cannot be verbally named because the right hemisphere lacks direct access to left-hemisphere speech centers. The left (categorical) hemisphere usually dominates sequential language processing and analytical calculation. The right (representational) hemisphere contributes more to visuospatial awareness, three-dimensional construction, facial recognition, musical prosody and emotional tone of speech.

open.q: Contrast the primary cognitive specializations of the left (categorical) hemisphere versus the right (representational) hemisphere.
accept: Left hemisphere: language (speech, comprehension, reading, writing) and analytical/sequential reasoning; Right hemisphere: visuospatial processing, facial recognition, prosody/emotional tone, and spatial attention

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: What is 'hemispatial neglect' (contralateral neglect syndrome), and which cortical lesion most commonly produces it?
options: Right posterior parietal damage causes left-sided neglect despite intact primary vision
Left posterior parietal damage causes right-sided neglect with primary blindness
Right occipital damage causes left-sided neglect by interrupting the optic nerve
Cerebellar vermis damage causes neglect of the left side of the body
questions.explain: Because the right parietal lobe attends to BOTH left and right visual hemispaces whereas the left parietal lobe attends primarily to the right hemispace, right parietal damage leaves left hemispace unattended. Patients may eat only food on the right half of a plate, shave only the right side of the face, or draw only the right half of a clock. The right parietal lobe attends to both hemispaces, whereas the left attends mainly to right hemispace.

open.q: Identify the cortical region most commonly damaged in left hemispatial neglect and describe two classic behavioral signs of the syndrome.
accept: Right posterior parietal cortex (non-dominant parietal lobe); patient ignores the left side of space/body (e.g., eats food only from the right side of the plate, draws numbers only on the right half of a clock face, or shaves/dresses only the right side)
Right parietal lobe; ignoring left side of plate/clock/body despite intact vision

questions.q: Match the specific thalamic relay nuclei with their sensory/motor inputs and cortical targets:
options: VPL: body → S1; VPM: face/taste → S1; LGN: vision → V1; MGN: audition → A1; VA/VL: basal ganglia/cerebellum → motor cortex
VPL: face/taste → S1; VPM: body → S1; LGN: audition → A1; MGN: vision → V1; VA/VL: basal ganglia/cerebellum → motor cortex
VPL: body → motor cortex; VPM: face → visual cortex; LGN: vision → auditory cortex; MGN: audition → S1; VA/VL: spinal cord → cerebellum
VPL: vision → V1; VPM: audition → A1; LGN: body → S1; MGN: face → S1; VA/VL: taste → insula
questions.explain: Quick mnemonics: LGN = Light (vision), MGN = Music (audition), VPM = Makeup/Mouth (face somatosensation & taste), VPL = Limbs/body somatosensation. VPL relays body somatosensation via the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract; VPM relays facial sensation and taste; LGN relays vision; MGN relays audition; VA/VL relay basal ganglia and cerebellar output to motor and premotor cortex.

open.q: State the input pathway and cortical target for: (1) VPL, (2) VPM, (3) Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN), and (4) Medial Geniculate Nucleus (MGN).
accept: 1) VPL: dorsal columns & spinothalamic tract -> S1 (body); 2) VPM: trigeminal & taste pathways -> S1 (face/taste); 3) LGN: optic tract -> primary visual cortex (V1); 4) MGN: inferior colliculus -> primary auditory cortex (A1)
VPL (body somatosensory -> S1), VPM (face/taste -> S1), LGN (vision -> V1), MGN (audition -> A1)

questions.q: What is 'Dejerine-Roussy syndrome' (central post-stroke thalamic pain syndrome)?
options: Contralateral VPL/VPM thalamic stroke causes delayed burning pain and allodynia
Ipsilateral occipital infarction causes painless visual loss
Bilateral hippocampal injury causes fluent aphasia
Cerebellar peduncle infarction causes isolated resting tremor
questions.explain: Maladaptive neuroplasticity and loss of GABAergic thalamic reticular inhibition in deafferented VPL/VPM relay neurons generate excruciating central neuropathic pain. After a contralateral VPL/VPM thalamic stroke, initial sensory loss may be followed weeks or months later by severe burning dysesthesia, allodynia and hyperpathia, often triggered by light touch or temperature.

open.q: Describe the clinical presentation and anatomical lesion site of Dejerine-Roussy syndrome.
accept: Severe, intractable burning contralateral pain and allodynia developing weeks after a thalamic stroke involving the ventral posterolateral/posteromedial (VPL/VPM) nuclei
Contralateral thalamic (VPL/VPM) stroke causing delayed severe central burning pain/allodynia

questions.q: What is the physiological generator of the scalp Electroencephalogram (EEG) signal?
options: Summated EPSPs and IPSPs in synchronously active cortical pyramidal-cell dendrites
Action potentials travelling in deep thalamic axons
Motor-unit potentials from scalp and facial muscles
Pulsatile blood flow in cortical and dural vessels
questions.explain: Because action potentials are brief (~1 ms) and asynchronous, they cancel out at the scalp, whereas longer-lasting (~15-200 ms) dendritic postsynaptic potentials sum into measurable microvolt (~10-100 uV) scalp EEG waves. EEG reflects summed extracellular postsynaptic potentials in aligned cortical pyramidal-cell dendrites. Brief, asynchronous action potentials largely cancel at the scalp, whereas longer-lasting dendritic potentials can summate into measurable signals.

open.q: Which electrical events and cortical neurons generate the voltage fluctuations recorded on a scalp EEG?
accept: Synchronous summated excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs) in the apical dendrites of vertically aligned cortical pyramidal neurons
Summated postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs/IPSPs) of cortical pyramidal cell dendrites

questions.q: Match the four classic physiological EEG frequency bands with their frequencies (Hz) and behavioral states:
options: Beta >13 Hz: alert/REM; alpha 8–13 Hz: relaxed, eyes closed; theta 4–7 Hz: drowsy/N1; delta <4 Hz: deep N3
Beta 4–7 Hz: deep N3; alpha >30 Hz: alert; theta 8–13 Hz: relaxed; delta 13–30 Hz: REM
Beta >13 Hz: relaxed, eyes closed; alpha 8–13 Hz: deep N3; theta <4 Hz: alert; delta 4–7 Hz: REM
Beta <4 Hz: deep N3; alpha 4–7 Hz: N1; theta 13–30 Hz: alert; delta 8–13 Hz: relaxed
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'BATS Drink Blood' from awake/REM to deep sleep: Beta (>13 Hz) -> Alpha (8-13 Hz) -> Theta (4-7 Hz) -> Sleep spindles/K-complexes (N2) -> Delta (<4 Hz, N3). Beta activity is low-amplitude and fast; alpha is maximal over parieto-occipital cortex with eyes closed; theta appears in drowsiness and N1; delta dominates deep N3 sleep. REM EEG is desynchronised and resembles wakefulness.

open.q: State the frequency range (in Hz) and the characteristic awake/sleep state for: (1) Beta waves, (2) Alpha waves, (3) Theta waves, and (4) Delta waves.
accept: 1) Beta (>13-30 Hz): alert awake/concentrating or REM sleep; 2) Alpha (8-13 Hz): relaxed awake with eyes closed; 3) Theta (4-7 Hz): drowsiness / stage N1 sleep; 4) Delta (<4 Hz): deep slow-wave sleep (stage N3)
Beta >13 Hz (alert/REM), Alpha 8-13 Hz (relaxed eyes closed), Theta 4-7 Hz (N1), Delta <4 Hz (N3 deep sleep)

questions.q: What is 'alpha block' (alpha desynchronization / Berger effect) on an EEG?
options: Opening the eyes or mental effort suppresses alpha and produces low-voltage beta activity
Opening the eyes increases alpha amplitude and suppresses beta activity
Closing the eyes replaces alpha with high-amplitude delta waves
Mental effort produces generalised 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges
questions.explain: Sensory input or cognitive effort desynchronizes thalamocortical alpha pacemakers into fast, low-amplitude beta waves (also called arousal or orienting response). In a relaxed awake person with eyes closed, prominent 8–13 Hz occipital alpha activity is present. Visual input or cognitive effort desynchronises this rhythm, replacing it with low-voltage, higher-frequency beta activity.

open.q: Describe what happens to the occipital alpha rhythm on an EEG when a relaxed subject opens their eyes ('alpha block').
accept: The high-amplitude 8-13 Hz alpha rhythm is immediately replaced ('desynchronized') by low-amplitude, high-frequency (>13 Hz) beta waves
Alpha waves disappear and shift to fast, low-voltage beta activity

questions.q: Which EEG waveform is pathognomonic for typical childhood 'absence (petit mal) seizures', and which ion channel is targeted by first-line ethosuximide therapy?
options: Generalised 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges; ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels
Generalised 1-Hz periodic sharp waves; ethosuximide blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels
Focal temporal spikes; ethosuximide activates GABA-A receptors
High-amplitude delta waves; ethosuximide blocks NMDA receptors
questions.explain: Hyperventilation for 3 minutes classically provokes the diagnostic 3 Hz spike-and-wave bursts in absence epilepsy, driven by thalamic T-type Ca2+ channel pacemaker oscillations. Typical absence seizures produce abrupt, generalised, symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Ethosuximide reduces thalamocortical burst activity by blocking low-threshold T-type calcium channels; hyperventilation may provoke the pattern.

open.q: State the classic EEG pattern of absence seizures and the specific thalamic ion channel blocked by ethosuximide.
accept: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges; thalamic T-type calcium (Ca2+) channels
3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern; T-type Ca2+ channels

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: Match the stages of human sleep (NREM stages N1, N2, N3, and REM sleep) with their characteristic EEG features:
options: N1: theta; N2: sleep spindles/K-complexes; N3: delta; REM: desynchronised EEG with atonia
N1: sleep spindles; N2: delta; N3: beta; REM: high-amplitude theta with muscle tone
N1: delta; N2: flat EEG; N3: sleep spindles; REM: synchronised alpha with atonia
N1: beta; N2: rapid eye movements; N3: theta; REM: K-complexes and muscle tone
questions.explain: Sleep spindles and K-complexes are the hallmark EEG signatures of Stage N2 sleep, which constitutes roughly half of adult nocturnal sleep. N1 features theta waves, vertex sharp waves and slow eye movements. N2 features 12–14 Hz sleep spindles and K-complexes and occupies about 45–50% of sleep. N3 has high-amplitude delta waves. REM has rapid eye movements, skeletal muscle atonia and a desynchronised, sawtooth/beta-like EEG.

open.q: Identify the specific sleep stage characterized by: (1) sleep spindles and K-complexes, (2) high-amplitude delta waves, and (3) desynchronized EEG with skeletal muscle atonia.
accept: 1) Stage N2 NREM sleep; 2) Stage N3 (slow-wave) NREM sleep; 3) REM sleep

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: Compare the physiological changes (brain metabolism, autonomic tone, muscle tone, dreaming, and timing across the night) in NREM slow-wave sleep versus REM sleep:
options: NREM: reduced cerebral activity with preserved tone; REM: active dreaming, variable autonomic activity and skeletal muscle atonia
NREM: vivid dreams with muscle atonia; REM: slow waves, stable autonomic tone and increased muscle tone
NREM and REM both have identical EEG, autonomic and muscle activity
REM occurs only in the first part of the night and becomes shorter toward morning
questions.explain: REM sleep is called 'paradoxical sleep' because the EEG and cerebral metabolic rate resemble active wakefulness while the sleeper is hardest to arouse and skeletal muscles are actively paralyzed.

open.q: Contrast NREM slow-wave sleep and REM sleep across four parameters: EEG activity, skeletal muscle tone, autonomic stability, and timing across a normal night.
accept: NREM: high-voltage synchronized delta waves, preserved muscle tone, stable parasympathetic dominance, predominates in early night; REM: low-voltage desynchronized beta/sawtooth waves, active skeletal muscle atonia (except diaphragm/extraocular), irregular autonomic variability, lengthens in late morning cycles (~90-min ultradian rhythm)
Delta waves/preserved tone/stable parasympathetic/early night (NREM) vs desynchronized EEG/muscle atonia/variable autonomic/late night (REM)

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: Which hypothalamic nuclei and neurotransmitters regulate the circadian sleep-wake 'flip-flop switch' and REM sleep generation?
options: SCN sets circadian timing; VLPO promotes sleep via GABA/galanin; orexin stabilises wakefulness; pontine cholinergic circuits promote REM
SCN initiates REM directly; VLPO promotes wakefulness; orexin suppresses arousal; pontine nuclei generate melatonin
Suprachiasmatic nucleus produces GABA for NREM; cerebellum releases orexin for wakefulness
All sleep stages are controlled exclusively by the pineal gland
questions.explain: Mutual inhibition between sleep-promoting VLPO (GABA/galanin) and wake-promoting monoaminergic/histaminergic/cholinergic nuclei forms a bistable 'flip-flop' switch stabilized by orexin (hypocretin).

open.q: State the roles of: (1) the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), (2) the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO), and (3) lateral hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons in sleep-wake regulation.
accept: 1) SCN: master circadian pacemaker entrained by light that regulates melatonin and sleep timing; 2) VLPO: releases GABA/galanin to inhibit arousal centers and initiate NREM sleep; 3) Orexin neurons: excite arousal centers to stabilize wakefulness and prevent inappropriate transitions into REM sleep
SCN (circadian clock), VLPO (GABA/galanin sleep promoter), orexin (stabilizes wakefulness)

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: What is the pathophysiological basis of 'Narcolepsy with Cataplexy', and why do patients experience sudden emotionally triggered muscle collapse (cataplexy), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations?
options: Loss of hypothalamic orexin destabilises wakefulness, allowing REM features to intrude
Excess pituitary melatonin suppresses REM sleep and causes cataplexy
Cerebellar Purkinje-cell loss causes REM atonia during wakefulness
Increased spinal corticospinal activity causes emotionally triggered paralysis
questions.explain: Low or undetectable CSF hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) is diagnostic of narcolepsy type 1, strongly associated with HLA-DQB1*06:02. Narcolepsy type 1 is associated with loss of orexin (hypocretin)-producing lateral hypothalamic neurons. This destabilises sleep-wake control, allowing REM-related muscle atonia and dream phenomena to intrude into wakefulness; low CSF hypocretin supports the diagnosis.

open.q: Name the deficient hypothalamic neuropeptide in narcolepsy with cataplexy and explain how its loss causes cataplexy.
accept: Orexin (hypocretin); loss of orexin destabilizes the sleep-wake switch, allowing REM-sleep descending glycinergic skeletal muscle atonia to intrude suddenly into wakefulness during strong emotions (laughter/surprise)
Orexin (hypocretin) deficiency; inappropriate intrusion of REM muscle atonia into wakefulness

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: How do 'REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD)' and 'Somnambulism (sleepwalking) / Night Terrors' differ in their sleep stage of occurrence and pathophysiology?
options: RBD: REM sleep with loss of atonia; sleepwalking/night terrors: N3 arousal parasomnias
RBD: N3 sleep with loss of atonia; sleepwalking: REM dream enactment
Both occur during N1 sleep and result from excess alpha activity
RBD occurs during wakefulness; sleepwalking occurs during REM atonia
questions.explain: Over 80% of older adults with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder eventually develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy. REM sleep behaviour disorder involves failure of normal brainstem-mediated REM atonia, allowing dream enactment. Sleepwalking and night terrors are partial arousals from N3 slow-wave sleep and are commonly followed by amnesia.

open.q: Contrast REM Sleep Behavior Disorder and sleepwalking (somnambulism) in terms of sleep stage and underlying mechanism.
accept: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder: occurs in REM sleep due to loss of normal brainstem-mediated skeletal muscle atonia, leading to dream enactment (associated with alpha-synucleinopathies); Sleepwalking: occurs during Stage N3 slow-wave sleep as a partial NREM arousal disorder with amnesia
REM sleep with lost muscle atonia/dream enactment (RBD) vs Stage N3 slow-wave arousal disorder (sleepwalking)

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: Compare 'Broca's (expressive/non-fluent) aphasia' and 'Wernicke's (receptive/fluent) aphasia' in terms of lesion site, speech fluency, comprehension, and repetition:
options: Broca: left inferior frontal, non-fluent; comprehension intact, repetition impaired. Wernicke: left posterior temporal, fluent; comprehension and repetition impaired
Broca: left posterior temporal, fluent; comprehension impaired. Wernicke: left inferior frontal, non-fluent; comprehension intact
Broca and Wernicke: fluent speech, intact comprehension and impaired repetition
Broca: right occipital, non-fluent; Wernicke: right parietal, fluent; both have intact repetition
questions.explain: Because Broca's area sits right next to the primary motor cortex face/arm area, Broca's aphasia is frequently accompanied by right face/arm weakness, whereas Wernicke's aphasia often has no hemiparesis (or a right superior quadrantanopia). Broca's aphasia produces effortful, telegraphic speech with awareness of the deficit; Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent but paraphasic or meaningless speech, often with poor insight. Both typically impair repetition. Broca's area is in the left inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann 44/45); Wernicke's area is in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (area 22).

open.q: Contrast Broca's aphasia and Wernicke's aphasia across four features: anatomical site, speech fluency, auditory comprehension, and repetition.
accept: Broca's: left inferior frontal gyrus, non-fluent/telegraphic speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition; Wernicke's: left posterior superior temporal gyrus, fluent/paraphasic ('word salad') speech, impaired comprehension, impaired repetition
Left inferior frontal/non-fluent/comprehension intact (Broca) vs left superior temporal/fluent meaningless/comprehension impaired (Wernicke)

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: What is 'Conduction Aphasia', which white matter tract is damaged, and what is its hallmark clinical profile?
options: Arcuate fasciculus lesion: fluent speech, intact comprehension, severely impaired repetition
Arcuate fasciculus lesion: non-fluent speech, poor comprehension, preserved repetition
Corpus callosum lesion: fluent speech, poor comprehension, normal repetition
Internal capsule lesion: non-fluent speech, intact comprehension, absent spontaneous speech
questions.explain: In the Wernicke-Geschwind model, repeating spoken words requires Wernicke's area -> Arcuate Fasciculus -> Broca's area; interrupting the arcuate fasciculus selectively abolishes repetition while leaving comprehension and spontaneous speech intact. The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke's and Broca's areas. Damage produces phonemic paraphasias and severe repetition impairment despite relatively preserved spontaneous fluency and auditory comprehension; patients may make repeated self-corrections (conduite d'approche).

open.q: Name the white matter tract damaged in Conduction Aphasia and state the status of fluency, comprehension, and repetition.
accept: Arcuate fasciculus; fluent spontaneous speech, intact comprehension, and severely impaired repetition
Arcuate fasciculus; fluent speech + intact comprehension + impaired repetition

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: How do 'Transcortical Motor Aphasia' and 'Transcortical Sensory Aphasia' differ from Broca's and Wernicke's aphasias?
options: Transcortical aphasias preserve repetition; perisylvian aphasias impair it
Transcortical aphasias impair repetition; perisylvian aphasias preserve it
Both groups preserve repetition because the arcuate fasciculus is intact
Both groups impair repetition because all language pathways are interrupted
questions.explain: Diagnostic algorithm for aphasias: 1) Check Repetition (impaired = Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global; intact = Transcortical); 2) Check Fluency; 3) Check Comprehension. Transcortical aphasias usually follow watershed lesions that spare the perisylvian language loop, so repetition is preserved and echolalia may occur. Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction and global aphasias generally impair repetition.

open.q: Which single bedside language test reliably distinguishes transcortical aphasias from perisylvian aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction)?
accept: Repetition (repetition is preserved in transcortical aphasias because the perisylvian Wernicke-arcuate-Broca circuit remains intact, whereas repetition is impaired in perisylvian aphasias)
Repetition (intact in transcortical aphasias, impaired in perisylvian aphasias)

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: What is 'Alexia without Agraphia' (pure word blindness), and which vascular occlusion produces it?
options: Left PCA infarct involving left occipital cortex and splenium causes alexia without agraphia
Right PCA infarct involving right occipital cortex and genu causes agraphia without alexia
Left MCA infarct involving Broca's area causes pure word blindness
Anterior communicating artery rupture causes inability to recognise spoken words
questions.explain: Alexia without agraphia is the classic disconnection syndrome described by Dejerine: left occipital lobe + splenium of corpus callosum infarction from a left PCA stroke. The left occipital lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia; splenial damage prevents visual information reaching left-hemisphere language areas from the intact right visual cortex. The patient can write but cannot read, including what they have just written.

open.q: Identify the occluded artery and the two damaged neuroanatomical structures that produce 'alexia without agraphia' (pure word blindness).
accept: Left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA); left visual (occipital) cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum
Left PCA; left occipital cortex and splenium of corpus callosum

questions.sub: Memory Systems, Hippocampus, and Synaptic Plasticity (LTP)
questions.q: How are human memory systems classified by duration and conscious awareness (declarative/explicit vs non-declarative/implicit)?
options: Working: prefrontal; explicit: hippocampal/neocortical; implicit: basal ganglia, cerebellum and amygdala
Working: hippocampal; explicit: spinal; implicit: prefrontal and thalamic
Working: cerebellar; explicit: basal ganglia; implicit: hippocampal only
Working: amygdala; explicit: cerebellar; implicit: medial temporal only
questions.explain: Patient H.M. (bilateral medial temporal lobe/hippocampal resection) developed profound anterograde amnesia for new declarative facts/events while retaining intact working memory, old childhood memories, and new procedural motor learning (mirror-drawing). Working memory depends heavily on prefrontal networks. Explicit (declarative) memory includes episodic and semantic memory and requires the hippocampus/medial temporal lobe for consolidation into neocortex. Implicit memory includes procedural skills (basal ganglia/cerebellum), priming (neocortex) and conditioning (amygdala/cerebellum).

open.q: Contrast explicit (declarative) memory and implicit (non-declarative) memory in terms of conscious awareness, subtypes, and primary brain structures.
accept: Explicit (declarative): conscious recall of episodic events and semantic facts, dependent on hippocampus/medial temporal lobe for consolidation and neocortex for long-term storage; Implicit (non-declarative): unconscious memory including procedural motor skills (basal ganglia/cerebellum), emotional conditioning (amygdala), and priming (neocortex)
Conscious facts/events via hippocampus/neocortex (explicit) vs unconscious motor skills/conditioning via basal ganglia/cerebellum/amygdala (implicit)

questions.sub: Memory Systems, Hippocampus, and Synaptic Plasticity (LTP)
questions.q: What is the cellular mechanism of 'Long-Term Potentiation (LTP)' in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons (Schaffer collateral synapses)?
options: AMPA depolarisation removes the NMDA Mg2+ block; Ca2+ influx activates CaMKII and strengthens synapses
NMDA inhibition prevents Ca2+ entry and removes postsynaptic AMPA receptors
GABA-A activation opens chloride channels and permanently increases glutamate release
Presynaptic dopamine blocks AMPA receptors and suppresses dendritic growth
questions.explain: NMDA receptors act as Hebbian 'coincidence detectors' requiring BOTH presynaptic glutamate binding AND postsynaptic depolarization (to remove Mg2+) before Ca2+ influx triggers synaptic strengthening. High-frequency glutamate release activates AMPA receptors, depolarising the postsynaptic spine and expelling the voltage-dependent Mg2+ block from NMDA receptors. NMDA-mediated Ca2+ entry activates CaMKII, promoting AMPA-receptor insertion (early LTP) and CREB-mediated gene transcription and spine remodelling (late LTP).

open.q: Explain the sequential roles of AMPA receptors, Mg2+ ions, NMDA receptors, and Ca2+/CaMKII in hippocampal Long-Term Potentiation (LTP).
accept: Glutamate activates AMPA receptors to depolarize the postsynaptic membrane, expelling Mg2+ from NMDA receptor channels; Ca2+ influx through NMDA receptors activates CaMKII, which promotes AMPA receptor insertion and structural synaptic strengthening
AMPA depolarization expels Mg2+ from NMDA channels -> Ca2+ influx -> CaMKII activation -> new AMPA receptor insertion

questions.sub: Limbic System, Papez Circuit, and Amygdala
questions.q: Trace the anatomical loop of the 'Papez Circuit' involved in emotion and declarative memory consolidation:
options: Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamus → cingulate gyrus → entorhinal cortex
Hippocampus → internal capsule → caudate → red nucleus → cerebellum
Amygdala → optic tract → lateral geniculate → calcarine cortex → hippocampus
Cingulate gyrus → corticospinal tract → spinal cord → mammillary bodies → hippocampus
questions.explain: Damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial/anterior thalamus in thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) disrupts the Papez circuit, producing severe anterograde/retrograde amnesia and confabulation. The Papez circuit runs from the hippocampal formation through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, then via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex before returning to the hippocampus.

open.q: List the sequential structures of the Papez circuit starting and ending at the hippocampus.
accept: Hippocampus -> Fornix -> Mammillary bodies -> Mammillothalamic tract -> Anterior thalamic nucleus -> Cingulate gyrus -> Entorhinal cortex -> Hippocampus
Hippocampus -> fornix -> mammillary bodies -> anterior thalamus -> cingulate gyrus -> entorhinal cortex -> hippocampus

questions.sub: Limbic System, Papez Circuit, and Amygdala
questions.q: What is 'Kluver-Bucy syndrome', and which bilateral brain lesion produces it?
options: Bilateral amygdala damage causes placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality and visual agnosia
Unilateral Broca-area damage causes hyperorality, aphasia and visual agnosia
Bilateral caudate damage causes chorea, disinhibition and loss of fear
Occipital cortex damage causes hypersexuality, placidity and facial blindness
questions.explain: Because HSV-1 encephalitis has a strong tropism for the inferior frontal and anterior temporal lobes (including the amygdala and hippocampus), bilateral temporal necrosis can produce Kluver-Bucy syndrome. Klüver–Bucy syndrome follows bilateral amygdala/anterior temporal damage. Features include placidity or loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality and visual agnosia; herpes simplex encephalitis is a recognised cause.

open.q: Name the brain structure whose bilateral damage causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome and list four hallmark behavioral features.
accept: Bilateral amygdala (anterior temporal lobes); placidity/tameness (loss of fear), hyperorality, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia
Bilateral amygdala; placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, visual agnosia

questions.sub: Memory Systems, Hippocampus, and Synaptic Plasticity (LTP)
questions.q: What is 'Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome', what nutritional deficiency precipitates it, and how do its acute reversible triad and chronic amnestic features differ?
options: Thiamine deficiency causes acute Wernicke triad and chronic Korsakoff amnesia/confabulation
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes acute ophthalmoplegia and chronic chorea
Vitamin C deficiency causes acute confusion and chronic retrograde amnesia
Copper excess causes acute ataxia and chronic aphasia
questions.explain: Always administer intravenous THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE in malnourished or alcoholic patients, because a glucose load rapidly consumes remaining thiamine-dependent pyruvate dehydrogenase/transketolase cofactors and precipitates acute Wernicke encephalopathy! Wernicke encephalopathy presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and gait ataxia. Chronic Korsakoff syndrome causes severe anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation; mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus are commonly affected. Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients.

open.q: State the vitamin deficiency, acute clinical triad, chronic memory hallmark, and damaged diencephalic structures in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
accept: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency; Acute triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia; Chronic: severe anterograde/retrograde amnesia with confabulation; Structures: mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus
Thiamine (B1); confusion/ophthalmoplegia/ataxia; amnesia + confabulation; mammillary bodies & dorsomedial thalamus

questions.sub: Hypothalamus: Autonomic, Endocrine, Feeding, and Thermoregulatory Nuclei
questions.q: Match the major hypothalamic nuclei with their specific physiological functions:
options: Supraoptic/PVN: ADH and oxytocin; SCN: circadian rhythm; anterior: cooling; posterior: heat; VMN: satiety; lateral: hunger
Supraoptic/PVN: growth hormone; SCN: feeding; anterior: heat conservation; posterior: cooling; VMN: hunger; lateral: satiety
Supraoptic/PVN: prolactin; SCN: thermoregulation; anterior: hunger; posterior: satiety; VMN: cooling; lateral: heat
Supraoptic/PVN: ACTH; SCN: sleep induction only; anterior: satiety; posterior: hunger; VMN: heat; lateral: cooling
questions.explain: Classic mnemonics: 'Anterior = A/C (cooling)', 'Ventromedial = Very Massive (lesion causes obesity)', 'Lateral = Lean/starving (lesion causes anorexia)'. The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei synthesise ADH and oxytocin; the suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian pacemaker. The anterior hypothalamus promotes heat loss, the posterior conserves heat, the ventromedial nucleus supports satiety, and the lateral area promotes feeding and orexin-mediated arousal.

open.q: Match the hypothalamic nuclei with their functions: (1) Anterior nucleus, (2) Posterior nucleus, (3) Ventromedial nucleus, and (4) Lateral hypothalamic area.
accept: 1) Anterior: heat dissipation / cooling; 2) Posterior: heat conservation / thermogenesis; 3) Ventromedial: satiety center; 4) Lateral: hunger/feeding center and orexin arousal

questions.sub: Hypothalamus: Autonomic, Endocrine, Feeding, and Thermoregulatory Nuclei
questions.q: How do 'leptin' and 'ghrelin' act antagonistically on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to regulate appetite and energy balance?
options: Leptin activates POMC/CART and inhibits NPY/AgRP; ghrelin activates NPY/AgRP
Leptin activates NPY/AgRP and inhibits POMC/CART; ghrelin activates POMC/CART
Both hormones activate POMC/CART and suppress hunger
Both hormones inhibit NPY/AgRP and stimulate feeding
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Ghrelin makes your stomach growl' (fasting hunger hormone activating NPY/AgRP), while 'Leptin makes you lean' (adipose satiety hormone activating POMC/alpha-MSH). Leptin is released by adipocytes in proportion to fat stores; it promotes anorexigenic POMC/CART activity and inhibits orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons. Ghrelin is released by the stomach during fasting and activates NPY/AgRP neurons to stimulate hunger.

open.q: Contrast the tissue source, nutritional trigger, and arcuate nucleus neuronal targets of leptin versus ghrelin.
accept: Leptin: secreted by adipocytes when fat stores are high, activates anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons (suppresses appetite) and inhibits NPY/AgRP; Ghrelin: secreted by the stomach during fasting, activates orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons (stimulates hunger)
Adipose satiety hormone activating POMC/inhibiting NPY-AgRP (leptin) vs gastric fasting hunger hormone activating NPY-AgRP (ghrelin)

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: Trace the normal production, circulation pathway, and venous absorption of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF):
options: Choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → Monro → third → aqueduct → fourth → Magendie/Luschka → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations
Choroid plexus → fourth ventricle → aqueduct → third → Monro → lateral ventricles → central canal
Lateral ventricles → Luschka → third ventricle → Magendie → aqueduct → subarachnoid space
Choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → cerebral aqueduct → Monro → fourth ventricle → venous sinuses
questions.explain: Because CSF is produced at ~500 mL/day (~20 mL/hr) while total subarachnoid/ventricular volume is ~150 mL, CSF turns over roughly 3 to 4 times every 24 hours. CSF is produced mainly by choroid plexuses (~500 mL/day; total volume ~130–150 mL). It flows through the foramina of Monro, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, and foramina of Magendie and Luschka into the subarachnoid space, then returns to dural venous sinuses via arachnoid villi/granulations.

open.q: Trace the anatomical pathway of CSF flow from the lateral ventricles to its site of venous reabsorption, and state the daily production rate and total volume.
accept: Lateral ventricles -> foramina of Monro -> third ventricle -> cerebral aqueduct -> fourth ventricle -> foramina of Magendie & Luschka -> subarachnoid space -> arachnoid granulations -> superior sagittal sinus; ~500 mL/day production, ~150 mL total volume
Lateral -> Monro -> 3rd -> aqueduct -> 4th -> Magendie/Luschka -> subarachnoid space -> arachnoid granulations -> superior sagittal sinus (~500 mL/day, ~150 mL volume)

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: How do the anatomical basis and neuroprotective functions of the 'Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB)' differ from those of the 'Circumventricular Organs (CVOs)'?
options: BBB: tight endothelial junctions; CVOs: fenestrated capillaries expose blood signals to brain
BBB: fenestrated capillaries; CVOs: tight junctions exclude circulating hormones
BBB and CVOs have identical endothelial permeability
Astrocytes alone form the BBB; CVOs occur only in spinal cord
questions.explain: Circumventricular organs act as neuroendocrine and chemosensory 'windows' into the bloodstream (e.g., OVLT/SFO sense plasma hyperosmolarity and angiotensin II for thirst/ADH; area postrema senses emetic toxins). The BBB depends on non-fenestrated endothelial cells with tight junctions, basement membrane and astrocyte end-feet. Circumventricular organs have fenestrated capillaries and act as neuroendocrine or chemosensory windows, including the OVLT, subfornical organ and area postrema.

open.q: Name the three structural components of the blood-brain barrier and list three circumventricular organs that lack a blood-brain barrier.
accept: BBB components: non-fenestrated endothelial cells with tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte end-feet; Circumventricular organs: area postrema, organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT), subfornical organ (SFO), median eminence, neurohypophysis, pineal gland
Endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, astrocyte foot processes; area postrema, OVLT, subfornical organ

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: How do 'non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus', 'communicating hydrocephalus', and 'normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)' differ in mechanism and clinical presentation?
options: Obstructive: intraventricular blockage; communicating: impaired absorption; NPH: gait, urinary and cognitive triad
Obstructive: impaired arachnoid absorption; communicating: aqueductal blockage; NPH: acute raised-pressure syndrome
Obstructive: excess CSF production only; communicating: reduced production; NPH: isolated visual loss
All three result from cerebral atrophy and have identical mechanisms
questions.explain: Mnemonic for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) triad: 'Wet, wobbly, and wacky' (urinary incontinence, wide-based magnetic gait, cognitive decline)—reversible with CSF shunting. Non-communicating hydrocephalus results from a block within the ventricular system; communicating hydrocephalus usually reflects impaired CSF absorption. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is a chronic communicating form with gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline ('wet, wobbly, wacky').

open.q: Contrast non-communicating hydrocephalus and communicating hydrocephalus, and state the classic clinical triad of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH).
accept: Non-communicating: obstruction inside the ventricular system (e.g., aqueductal stenosis); Communicating: impaired CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations; NPH triad: gait disturbance (magnetic gait), urinary incontinence, and dementia
Intraventricular block vs impaired arachnoid absorption; NPH triad = gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, dementia

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: What is 'Gerstmann syndrome', and which specific cortical gyrus is lesioned?
options: Dominant angular gyrus lesion: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation
Non-dominant occipital lesion: agraphia, acalculia, prosopagnosia and neglect
Dominant precentral lesion: aphasia, hemianopia, anosmia and ataxia
Bilateral amygdala lesion: agraphia, acalculia, hyperorality and deafness
questions.explain: Whereas non-dominant (right) parietal lesions cause left hemispatial neglect, dominant (left) angular gyrus lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome. Gerstmann syndrome is associated with a lesion of the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule. Its classic features are agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation.

open.q: State the anatomical lesion site and the four hallmark clinical deficits of Gerstmann syndrome.
accept: Dominant (left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule; agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion
Left angular gyrus; agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: How do 'dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)' lesions and 'orbitofrontal cortex (OFC)' lesions differ in behavioral and executive dysfunction?
options: DLPFC: executive dysfunction and apathy; OFC: disinhibition, impulsivity and poor social judgement
DLPFC: social disinhibition; OFC: isolated loss of working memory and planning
DLPFC: visual agnosia; OFC: receptive aphasia and deafness
DLPFC and OFC lesions both cause isolated contralateral hemiplegia
questions.explain: Prefrontal cortex subdivides functionally into Dorsolateral (cold cognitive executive control/working memory) and Orbitofrontal/Ventromedial (emotional regulation, impulse control, social behavior). DLPFC injury impairs working memory, planning, set-shifting and cognitive flexibility, sometimes causing abulia. Orbitofrontal injury impairs impulse control and social behaviour, causing disinhibition, impulsivity, loss of empathy and primitive frontal-release signs.

open.q: Contrast the clinical syndromes resulting from dorsolateral prefrontal cortex lesions versus orbitofrontal cortex lesions.
accept: DLPFC lesion: executive dysfunction, impaired working memory/planning/set-shifting, and apathy; Orbitofrontal lesion: behavioral disinhibition, impulsivity, socially inappropriate behavior, and primitive frontal release signs
Executive/working memory deficits (DLPFC) vs social disinhibition/impulsivity (orbitofrontal)

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: What are the distinct functional roles of the 'Supplementary Motor Area (SMA)' and the 'Premotor Cortex (PMA)' located in Brodmann area 6 anterior to M1?
options: SMA: internally generated sequences; premotor cortex: externally cued movements and posture
SMA: visually cued movements; premotor cortex: internally generated bimanual sequences
SMA: primary sensation; premotor cortex: language comprehension
SMA and premotor cortex both directly activate lower motor neurons without M1
questions.explain: Regional cerebral blood flow studies show that thinking about a complex finger sequence activates the SMA without M1, whereas executing the sequence activates both SMA and M1. The medial supplementary motor area helps plan internally generated, sequential and bimanual movements. The lateral premotor cortex helps select externally or sensory-cued movements and stabilise proximal posture.

open.q: Distinguish the roles of the Supplementary Motor Area (SMA) and Premotor Cortex (PMA) in motor planning.
accept: SMA (medial area 6): internally generated, sequential, and bimanual motor planning; Premotor cortex (lateral area 6): externally/visually cued movement guidance and proximal limb stabilization
Internal sequential motor planning (SMA) vs sensory/externally cued movement guidance (premotor cortex)

questions.q: What is the unique inhibitory role of the 'Thalamic Reticular Nucleus (TRN)' in gating thalamocortical transmission?
options: GABAergic TRN inhibits thalamic relay nuclei, gating sensory transmission and generating N2 spindles
Glutamatergic TRN excites cortical pyramidal neurons and generates N3 delta waves
GABAergic TRN projects directly to spinal motor neurons to produce reflexes
TRN relays retinal signals directly to the primary visual cortex
questions.explain: Because every thalamocortical and corticothalamic axon passes through and sends collaterals to the GABAergic TRN, the TRN acts as an attentional 'searchlight' and generates 12-14 Hz sleep spindles. The thalamic reticular nucleus is a GABAergic shell around the lateral thalamus. It receives collaterals from thalamocortical and corticothalamic fibres and projects back to thalamic relay nuclei, contributing to sensory gating and N2 sleep spindles.

open.q: Name the thalamic nucleus that uses GABA to gate thalamic relay nuclei and generate 12-14 Hz sleep spindles.

questions.q: How do 'focal (partial) seizures' and 'generalized seizures' differ on EEG and clinically, and what is 'status epilepticus'?
options: Focal: one-hemisphere onset; generalized: bilateral onset; status: ≥5 min or no recovery between seizures
Focal: bilateral onset; generalized: one-hemisphere onset; status: any brief seizure
Focal: brainstem onset only; generalized: spinal onset only; status: two seizures with full recovery
Focal and generalized seizures differ only by duration; status requires a normal EEG
questions.explain: Prolonged status epilepticus (>5-30 min) causes excitotoxic glutamate-mediated neuronal death, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and lactic acidosis. Focal seizures begin within a network in one hemisphere; generalized seizures engage bilateral networks from onset. Status epilepticus is continuous seizure activity for at least 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without return to baseline consciousness.

open.q: Define status epilepticus and distinguish focal onset seizures from generalized onset seizures.
accept: Status epilepticus: continuous seizure lasting >=5 minutes or recurrent seizures without interictal return to baseline consciousness; Focal seizures arise within a localized network of one hemisphere, whereas generalized seizures engage bilateral networks simultaneously from onset
Seizure >=5 min or without consciousness recovery; localized unilateral onset (focal) vs simultaneous bilateral onset (generalized)

questions.q: Which EEG finding is characteristic of 'Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD)' (rapidly progressive prion dementia with startle myoclonus)?
options: Periodic synchronous bi- or triphasic sharp-wave complexes occurring every ~1 second (1 Hz) against a slowed background
Normal 11 Hz occipital alpha waves with intact alpha block
Isolated 14 Hz sleep spindles during wakefulness
3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges
questions.explain: Periodic 1 Hz sharp-wave complexes on EEG alongside rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and cortical ribboning on diffusion MRI strongly support sporadic CJD.

open.q: State the classic periodic EEG abnormality associated with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

questions.sub: Sleep Architecture: NREM Stages, REM Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
questions.q: Why does 'adenosine' accumulate in the basal forebrain during prolonged wakefulness, and how does caffeine promote alertness?
options: Adenosine builds sleep pressure during wakefulness; caffeine blocks A1/A2A receptors
Adenosine builds sleep pressure only during N3; caffeine activates A1/A2A receptors
Caffeine increases adenosine release and activates VLPO neurons
Adenosine blocks sleep-promoting neurons; caffeine stimulates GABA-A receptors
questions.explain: Homeostatic sleep drive (Process S) rises steadily during wakefulness via adenosine accumulation and clears during sleep, interacting with the circadian clock (Process C, SCN). ATP metabolism during wakefulness increases extracellular adenosine, contributing to homeostatic sleep pressure. Caffeine promotes alertness by competitively antagonising adenosine A1 and A2A receptors; sleep reduces the accumulated drive.

open.q: Explain the role of extracellular adenosine in homeostatic sleep drive and the receptor mechanism by which caffeine promotes wakefulness.
accept: Adenosine accumulates during wakefulness from ATP metabolism, inhibiting arousal neurons and promoting sleep pressure; caffeine competitively antagonizes adenosine (A1/A2A) receptors to block this sleep signal
Adenosine builds sleep pressure during wakefulness; caffeine blocks adenosine receptors

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: What is 'Prosopagnosia', and which specific cortical region is damaged?
options: Fusiform gyrus damage causes impaired familiar-face recognition despite intact vision
Primary visual cortex damage causes face blindness with preserved visual fields
Wernicke-area damage causes inability to recognise faces but preserves language
Facial nerve palsy causes visual agnosia and impaired object recognition
questions.explain: The fusiform face area on the ventral occipitotemporal 'what' visual stream is specialized for holistic facial recognition. Prosopagnosia is impaired recognition of familiar faces despite adequate basic vision. It is associated with bilateral or right-dominant lesions of the fusiform face area in the inferior occipitotemporal cortex.

open.q: Define prosopagnosia and name the specific gyrus damaged in this condition.
accept: Inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision; lesion of the fusiform gyrus (fusiform face area) in the inferior occipitotemporal cortex

questions.sub: Memory Systems, Hippocampus, and Synaptic Plasticity (LTP)
questions.q: Which basal forebrain cholinergic nucleus degenerates early in Alzheimer's disease, contributing to profound cholinergic deficit and cognitive/memory decline?
options: Nucleus basalis of Meynert, which provides widespread cortical acetylcholine
Locus coeruleus, which provides widespread cortical acetylcholine
Red nucleus, which provides widespread cortical dopamine
Inferior olive, which provides widespread cortical serotonin
questions.explain: Degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert and medial septal nucleus underpins the rationale for central cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease. Cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert project widely to the cerebral cortex, while the medial septal nucleus projects to the hippocampus. Their degeneration contributes to cholinergic deficits in Alzheimer's disease; central acetylcholinesterase inhibitors increase synaptic acetylcholine.

open.q: Name the basal forebrain cholinergic nucleus that degenerates in Alzheimer's disease and the drug class used to boost its synaptic neurotransmitter.
accept: Nucleus basalis of Meynert; central acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine)
Nucleus basalis of Meynert; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: How does normal Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) composition compare with arterial plasma in terms of protein, glucose, Cl-, Mg2+, K+, and Ca2+ concentrations?
options: CSF has low protein, glucose, K+ and Ca2+, but higher Cl− and Mg2+ than plasma
CSF has high protein, glucose, K+ and Ca2+, but lower Cl− and Mg2+ than plasma
CSF has the same protein and electrolyte composition as plasma
CSF normally contains abundant neutrophils and red blood cells
questions.explain: Because CSF is actively secreted by choroid plexus Na+/K+-ATPase and carbonic anhydrase transport (not a passive ultrafiltrate), it has higher Cl-/Mg2+ and lower K+/Ca2+/protein than plasma. Normal CSF has very low protein (~15–45 mg/dL), glucose around 60% of plasma, lower K+ and Ca2+, and slightly higher Cl− and Mg2+. It normally contains 0–5 lymphocytes/µL and no red blood cells.

open.q: Compare normal CSF versus blood plasma for: (1) protein concentration, (2) glucose concentration, (3) K+ concentration, and (4) Cl- concentration.
accept: 1) Protein: much lower in CSF (~15-45 mg/dL); 2) Glucose: lower in CSF (~60% of plasma glucose); 3) K+: lower in CSF; 4) Cl-: slightly higher in CSF
Much lower protein, ~60% glucose, lower K+, higher Cl-

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: What is the 'Monro-Kellie doctrine' of intracranial pressure (ICP), and what is the 'Cushing reflex' (Cushing triad) when ICP rises critically?
options: Rigid skull limits total brain/blood/CSF volume; raised ICP may cause hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing
Rigid skull permits brain volume to expand without displacing blood or CSF; raised ICP causes hypotension and tachycardia
Monro–Kellie describes spinal CSF pressure only; Cushing triad is hypotension, tachycardia and regular breathing
Cushing reflex is caused by low ICP and produces bradycardia, hypotension and apnoea
questions.explain: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = MAP - ICP. When rising ICP compresses brainstem arterioles, medullary ischemia triggers massive sympathetic vasoconstriction (raising MAP to preserve CPP), which then triggers carotid/aortic baroreceptor reflex bradycardia! The Monro–Kellie doctrine states that total intracranial volume (brain, blood and CSF) is constrained by the rigid skull. Rising ICP may trigger sympathetic hypertension to preserve cerebral perfusion, followed by baroreflex bradycardia and irregular respirations (Cushing triad).

open.q: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine and list the three components of Cushing's triad in severe intracranial hypertension.
accept: Monro-Kellie doctrine: the sum of intracranial volumes (brain + blood + CSF) is constant inside a rigid skull, so expansion of one requires displacement of another or ICP rises; Cushing triad: hypertension (widened pulse pressure), bradycardia, and irregular respirations
Constant total intracranial volume (brain + blood + CSF); hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing

questions.sub: Language Pathways and Aphasias (Broca, Wernicke, Conduction, Global)
questions.q: How do 'visual agnosia' (associative vs apperceptive), 'astereognosis', and 'apraxia' differ as higher cortical association deficits?
options: Visual agnosia: failed visual recognition; astereognosis: failed tactile recognition; apraxia: failed learned action
Visual agnosia: loss of acuity; astereognosis: anaesthesia; apraxia: flaccid paralysis
Visual agnosia: aphasia; astereognosis: deafness; apraxia: loss of proprioception
All three are primary sensory deficits caused by peripheral nerve lesions
questions.explain: All three reflect disconnection or damage to secondary/tertiary cortical association areas while primary sensory or motor cortex remains intact. Visual agnosia is failure to recognise objects by sight despite adequate basic vision; astereognosis is failure to identify an object by touch despite intact primary sensation; apraxia is inability to perform a learned purposeful action despite adequate strength and comprehension.

open.q: Define visual agnosia, astereognosis, and ideomotor apraxia.
accept: Visual agnosia: inability to recognize objects visually despite intact visual acuity; Astereognosis: inability to identify objects by touch alone despite intact primary somatosensation; Apraxia: inability to perform learned purposeful motor actions despite intact motor strength, coordination, and comprehension
Visual object recognition deficit, tactile object recognition deficit, learned motor execution deficit with intact strength

questions.sub: Limbic System, Papez Circuit, and Amygdala
questions.q: What are the physiological roles of the 'nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum)' and the 'mesolimbic dopamine pathway' from the Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA)?
options: VTA dopamine projections to nucleus accumbens support reward, motivation and reinforcement
Substantia nigra dopamine projections to spinal cord control nociception and reflexes
Locus coeruleus noradrenaline projections to nucleus accumbens suppress reward
Red nucleus glutamate projections to amygdala regulate renal function
questions.explain: Midbrain VTA dopamine neurons fire bursts when a reward is better than predicted (positive reward prediction error), reinforcing motivated behaviors and driving addiction neuroplasticity. The mesolimbic pathway originates in the ventral tegmental area and projects to the nucleus accumbens and other limbic regions. Dopamine signalling contributes to reward prediction, motivation, salience and reinforcement learning and is altered by addictive drugs.

open.q: Name the origin, target nucleus, primary neurotransmitter, and core behavioral function of the mesolimbic reward pathway.
accept: Origin: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA); Target: Nucleus accumbens (and amygdala/limbic structures); Neurotransmitter: Dopamine; Function: reward prediction, motivation, reinforcement learning, and addiction
VTA -> nucleus accumbens; dopamine; reward, motivation, and reinforcement

questions.sub: Hypothalamus: Autonomic, Endocrine, Feeding, and Thermoregulatory Nuclei
questions.q: What is 'Diabetes Insipidus' (central vs nephrogenic), and how does a lesion of the supraoptic/paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei or pituitary stalk affect plasma and urine osmolarity?
options: ADH deficiency or renal V2 resistance causes dilute polyuria, polydipsia and hypernatraemia
Excess ADH causes dilute polyuria, polydipsia and hypernatraemia
Insulin deficiency causes concentrated urine and reduced plasma osmolarity
Aldosterone deficiency causes anuria with highly concentrated urine
questions.explain: Central DI responds to exogenous desmopressin (DDAVP, a V2 agonist) with a >50% rise in urine osmolarity, whereas nephrogenic DI fails to concentrate urine after desmopressin. Central diabetes insipidus results from deficient ADH synthesis or release; nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance, often involving V2 receptors. Both impair collecting-duct water reabsorption, causing large volumes of dilute urine, thirst and possible hypernatraemia. Central DI responds to desmopressin.

open.q: State the hypothalamic nuclei damaged in central diabetes insipidus and the resulting changes in urine volume, urine osmolarity, and plasma sodium.
accept: Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei; massive polyuria, markedly decreased urine osmolarity (dilute urine), and hypernatremia / elevated plasma osmolarity
Supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei; polyuria, low urine osmolarity, hypernatremia

questions.sub: Cerebral Cortex Layers, Functional Areas, and Hemispheric Lateralization
questions.q: What is 'aphasia' versus 'dysarthria', and what is 'aprosodia' (expressive vs receptive)?
options: Aphasia: language disorder; dysarthria: motor articulation defect; aprosodia: impaired emotional prosody
Aphasia: vocal-cord disorder; dysarthria: impaired comprehension; aprosodia: loss of visual recognition
Aphasia: isolated memory loss; dysarthria: word-finding deficit; aprosodia: hearing loss
Aphasia: facial weakness; dysarthria: loss of grammar; aprosodia: inability to read
questions.explain: Right frontal lesions produce flat, monotone speech (expressive aprosodia), while right posterior temporal lesions impair recognizing emotion in others' voices (receptive aprosodia). Aphasia affects language formulation or comprehension. Dysarthria is impaired motor execution of speech with language intact. Aprosodia is loss of emotional melody or inflection: right frontal lesions may impair expression, while right posterior temporal lesions may impair recognition of emotion in others' speech.

open.q: Distinguish aphasia, dysarthria, and aprosodia in terms of their underlying neurological deficits.
accept: Aphasia: cortical language disorder affecting comprehension/production/grammar; Dysarthria: motor speech articulation disorder with intact language content; Aprosodia: inability to express or comprehend emotional tone/inflection of speech (right-hemisphere lesion)
Language disorder (aphasia), motor articulation defect (dysarthria), emotional speech melody defect (aprosodia)

questions.q: How is 'brain death' defined clinically and electrophysiologically?
options: Irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem functions, with absent brainstem reflexes and no respiratory drive on apnea testing
Loss of cortical awareness with preserved brainstem reflexes and spontaneous breathing
Severe quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements
Transient loss of consciousness with complete neurological recovery
questions.explain: Unlike persistent vegetative state (intact brainstem/hypothalamic sleep-wake cycles and spontaneous breathing, absent cortical awareness), brain death requires complete, irreversible absence of BOTH cortical and brainstem function. Clinical determination requires a known irreversible cause, coma, absence of brainstem reflexes and a positive apnea test under applicable clinical protocols. Ancillary testing, when indicated, may demonstrate electrocerebral silence or absent cerebral blood flow; a flat EEG alone does not establish brain death.

open.q: Contrast brain death versus persistent vegetative state in terms of brainstem function and EEG findings.
accept: Brain death: irreversible loss of BOTH cortical and brainstem functions (absent brainstem reflexes, positive apnea test, isoelectric flat EEG); Persistent vegetative state: loss of cortical awareness with preserved brainstem function (intact sleep-wake cycles, autonomic control, and spontaneous breathing)
Loss of both cortex & brainstem with flat EEG (brain death) vs loss of cortex with preserved brainstem/sleep-wake cycles (vegetative state)

questions.sub: Memory Systems, Hippocampus, and Synaptic Plasticity (LTP)
questions.q: How do 'anterograde amnesia' and 'retrograde amnesia' differ, and why does bilateral hippocampal damage spare distant childhood memories ('Ribot's law')?
options: Anterograde: impaired new learning; retrograde: loss of pre-injury memories; remote memories are relatively spared
Anterograde: loss of childhood memories; retrograde: inability to form new memories
Both terms describe loss of procedural motor skills after cerebellar injury
Hippocampal injury selectively erases remote memories while preserving recent memories
questions.explain: Ribot's gradient (recent memories are more vulnerable than remote consolidated memories after medial temporal damage) reflects gradual hippocampal-to-neocortical memory consolidation. Anterograde amnesia impairs formation of new long-term declarative memories; retrograde amnesia affects memories formed before injury. Remote memories are often less vulnerable because systems consolidation gradually distributes long-term storage across neocortical networks.

open.q: Distinguish anterograde amnesia from retrograde amnesia and explain why remote memories are preserved after hippocampal damage.
accept: Anterograde: inability to encode new declarative memories post-injury; Retrograde: loss of memories acquired prior to injury; remote memories are preserved because systems consolidation gradually shifts long-term storage from the hippocampus to the neocortex
Inability to form new memories (anterograde) vs loss of pre-injury memories (retrograde); remote memories are consolidated in the neocortex

questions.sub: CSF Production, Circulation, Blood-Brain Barrier, and Hydrocephalus
questions.q: What is 'Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)', who is the classic patient demographic, and what visual complication threatens permanent blindness?
options: Raised intracranial pressure with normal CSF/imaging; papilledema threatens vision
Low intracranial pressure with abnormal CSF; optic neuritis threatens vision
A posterior fossa mass obstructs the fourth ventricle and causes papilloedema
Bacterial meningitis causes low CSF glucose and bilateral retinal detachment
questions.explain: Treated with weight loss and acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces choroid plexus CSF secretion). Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects young women with obesity, with raised opening pressure, normal CSF composition and no mass lesion or hydrocephalus on imaging. Chronic papilloedema can cause optic atrophy and permanent visual loss. Weight loss and acetazolamide are commonly used treatments.

open.q: Define idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), name its primary vision-threatening sign, and explain how acetazolamide treats it.
accept: Elevated ICP with normal neuroimaging and normal CSF composition; papilledema (risking optic atrophy and blindness); acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus to decrease CSF production
Raised ICP with normal MRI/CSF; papilledema; acetazolamide reduces choroid plexus CSF secretion

questions.q: A 64-year-old right-handed man presents with sudden difficulty speaking after an ischemic stroke. His speech is slow, halting, and telegraphic ('Walk... dog... park'), omitting small grammatical connecting words, and he appears visibly frustrated by his errors. He follows three-step verbal commands accurately, cannot repeat 'No ifs, ands, or buts,' and has right facial droop and right arm weakness. Which artery and cortical area are infarcted?
options: Superior division of left MCA supplying Broca's area and adjacent motor cortex
Inferior division of left MCA supplying Wernicke's area and auditory cortex
Left PCA supplying the occipital visual cortex and splenium
Right ACA supplying the medial frontal and paracentral regions
questions.explain: Non-fluent telegraphic speech + intact comprehension + impaired repetition + right face/arm hemiparesis localizes to Broca's area and adjacent M1 (superior division of left MCA). Non-fluent telegraphic speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition and right face/arm weakness localise to Broca's area and adjacent primary motor cortex, supplied by the superior division of the left MCA.

open.q: Identify the aphasia type, cortical area, and occluded arterial branch in a patient with non-fluent telegraphic speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition, and right face/arm weakness.
accept: Broca's (expressive) aphasia; left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area, Brodmann 44/45); superior division of the left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)
Broca's aphasia; left inferior frontal gyrus; superior division of left MCA

questions.q: A 70-year-old right-handed woman is brought in because she suddenly began speaking in fluent, rapid, melodious sentences filled with nonsensical words and paraphasias ('The flibber drove the green telephone into the window') without realizing she makes no sense. She cannot follow simple spoken or written commands, cannot repeat phrases, and has no limb weakness. Which artery and cortical region are affected?
options: Inferior division of the Left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) supplying Wernicke's area (left posterior superior temporal gyrus, Brodmann 22)
Superior division of the Left MCA supplying Broca's area
Left Anterior Cerebral Artery
Left Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery
questions.explain: Fluent 'word salad' speech + impaired comprehension + impaired repetition + absence of motor hemiparesis is diagnostic of Wernicke's aphasia (inferior division of left MCA).

open.q: Identify the aphasia type, cortical region, and arterial branch occluded in a patient with fluent nonsensical speech ('word salad'), impaired comprehension, and no hemiparesis.
accept: Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia; left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area, Brodmann 22); inferior division of the left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)
Wernicke's aphasia; left posterior superior temporal gyrus; inferior division of left MCA

questions.q: A 66-year-old man undergoes evaluation after a small left parietal stroke. His spontaneous speech is fluent and grammatically normal, and he understands complex spoken and written instructions perfectly, yet when asked to repeat 'Methodist Episcopal' or 'Today is a sunny day,' he stumbles repeatedly with phonemic approximations ('Meth-episc... no, Medis...') and appears frustrated. What is his diagnosis and lesion location?
options: Conduction aphasia due to a lesion of the left Arcuate Fasciculus
Global aphasia due to complete left internal carotid occlusion
Broca's aphasia due to left inferior frontal infarct
Transcortical sensory aphasia
questions.explain: Intact fluency + intact comprehension + severely impaired repetition with phonemic self-correction is pathognomonic for conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus lesion).

open.q: Name the type of aphasia and the damaged white matter tract when spontaneous speech and comprehension are fluent/intact, but repetition is severely impaired.

questions.q: A 69-year-old hypertensive man has a left occipital lobe stroke. On examination, he has a right homonymous hemianopsia, writes a grammatically coherent paragraph on command without error, speaks and understands normally, yet is completely unable to read aloud the sentence he just wrote a minute earlier. Which artery is occluded and which corpus callosum structure is damaged?
options: Left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) damaging the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum (Alexia without agraphia)
Right Middle Cerebral Artery damaging the genu of the corpus callosum
Left Anterior Cerebral Artery damaging the paracentral lobule
Basilar artery damaging the basis pontis
questions.explain: Visual input reaches only the intact right visual cortex (due to left V1 damage) and is blocked from reaching left-hemisphere language centers by infarction of the splenium of the corpus callosum.

open.q: Name the syndrome, occluded artery, and commissural fiber bundle damaged when a patient can write normally but cannot read.
accept: Alexia without agraphia (pure word blindness); Left Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA); splenium of the corpus callosum
Alexia without agraphia; left PCA; splenium of corpus callosum

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman recovers from a right hemispheric stroke. When asked to draw a clock face, she crowds all numbers 1 through 12 onto the right half of the circle and leaves the left half blank; she eats food only from the right half of her tray and denies that her paralyzed left arm belongs to her (anosognosia). Which cortical region is damaged?
options: Right posterior parietal cortex (non-dominant inferior parietal lobule)
Left angular gyrus
Left primary visual cortex
Bilateral cerebellar hemispheres
questions.explain: Contralateral left hemispatial neglect and anosognosia localize to the right (non-dominant) posterior parietal cortex.

open.q: Which cerebral lobe and hemisphere are infarcted in a patient exhibiting left hemispatial neglect and anosognosia?
accept: Right posterior parietal lobe (non-dominant parietal cortex)

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated because his teacher notices he frequently stares blankly into space for 8-10 seconds several times per hour with subtle eyelid fluttering, does not respond when called during the episodes, and immediately resumes speaking mid-sentence without postictal confusion. Hyperventilation in the clinic reproduces the episode, and EEG shows abrupt-onset 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Which medication is indicated?
options: Ethosuximide (blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels)
Carbamazepine (which can worsen absence seizures)
Haloperidol
Atropine
questions.explain: Absence seizures have no postictal confusion, are provoked by hyperventilation, show 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG, and are treated first-line with ethosuximide (or valproate).

open.q: Name the seizure type, characteristic EEG frequency, and first-line drug mechanism in a child with brief staring spells, no postictal confusion, and hyperventilation-induced episodes.
accept: Typical absence (petit mal) seizure; generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges; ethosuximide (inhibits thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels)
Absence seizure; 3 Hz spike-and-wave; ethosuximide (T-type Ca2+ channel blocker)

questions.q: A 21-year-old college student presents with irresistible daytime sleep attacks, episodes where his knees buckle and he collapses to the floor for 30 seconds whenever he laughs hard at a joke (remaining fully conscious during the collapse), terrifying dream-like hallucinations as he falls asleep, and occasional inability to move for a minute upon waking. Polysomnography shows sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). What is the underlying neurochemical defect?
options: Loss of orexin (hypocretin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus
Excess dopamine in the substantia nigra
Destruction of the suprachiasmatic nucleus
Excess GABA in the locus coeruleus
questions.explain: The classic narcolepsy tetrad (excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis) is caused by hypocretin/orexin deficiency in the lateral hypothalamus.

open.q: State the diagnosis and deficient hypothalamic neuropeptide in a young adult with daytime sleep attacks, laughter-triggered cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations.
accept: Narcolepsy with cataplexy (Type 1 narcolepsy); deficiency of orexin (hypocretin) in the lateral hypothalamus

questions.q: A 67-year-old man is brought to the sleep clinic by his wife because over the past 2 years he has repeatedly punched, kicked, and yelled during the second half of the night while vividly dreaming of fighting off attackers, and awakens immediately alert recalling the dream. Polysomnography demonstrates loss of normal chin/limb EMG atonia during REM sleep. Which neurodegenerative disease class is he at high risk of developing?
options: Alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, or Multiple System Atrophy)
Huntington's disease
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Prion Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
questions.explain: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) reflects early alpha-synuclein pathology in pontomedullary REM-atonia nuclei (subcoeruleus / ventromedial medulla) years before overt Parkinsonian motor signs appear.

open.q: Name the sleep disorder characterized by dream enactment with loss of REM muscle atonia and identify the associated neurodegenerative proteinopathy.
accept: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD); alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy)
REM Sleep Behavior Disorder; alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson's / Lewy body dementia)

questions.q: A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department confused, with a wide-based staggering gait and horizontal nystagmus with bilateral lateral rectus palsy.
