Before his laboratory results return, he is given an IV infusion of 50% dextrose without vitamins, and his confusion worsens dramatically into permanent inability to form new memories, accompanied by confident fabrication of detailed stories about visiting Paris earlier that morning. Which brain structures suffered hemorrhagic necrosis?
options: Mammillary bodies and dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome precipitated by glucose administration prior to thiamine)
Bilateral caudate nuclei
Left inferior frontal gyrus
Cerebellar dentate nuclei
questions.explain: Administering glucose without thiamine depletes residual Vitamin B1 in thiamine-deficient patients, triggering acute Wernicke encephalopathy and irreversible Korsakoff psychosis (mammillary body and dorsomedial thalamic necrosis).

open.q: Which vitamin must always be given before IV dextrose in malnourished alcoholic patients to prevent hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus?

questions.q: A 76-year-old retired engineer is brought in by his family for progressive difficulty walking ('feet feel glued to the floor' with short shuffling steps), new-onset urinary incontinence, and worsening forgetfulness over 6 months. Brain MRI shows marked enlargement of all four cerebral ventricles out of proportion to cortical sulcal atrophy, and a large-volume lumbar puncture (opening pressure 14 cm H2O) dramatically improves his gait for 24 hours. What is the diagnosis?
options: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
Alzheimer's disease
Obstructive aqueductal stenosis
Subdural hematoma
questions.explain: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy + normal opening pressure + 'wet, wobbly, wacky' triad improving after high-volume CSF tap diagnoses NPH (treated with ventriculoperitoneal shunt).

open.q: Name the reversible cause of dementia, magnetic gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence characterized by ventriculomegaly with normal CSF opening pressure.

questions.q: A 61-year-old man who had a small lacunar stroke in the right thalamus 4 months ago returns complaining of agonizing, unremitting burning pain across the entire left side of his face, arm, and leg, exacerbated even by the light touch of a bedsheet. Examination shows decreased pinprick discrimination on the left side with severe tactile allodynia. Which specific thalamic nuclei were infarcted?
options: Right Ventral Posterolateral (VPL) and Ventral Posteromedial (VPM) nuclei (Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome)
Left Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
Right Medial Geniculate Nucleus (MGN)
Bilateral Anterior Thalamic Nuclei
questions.explain: Thalamogeniculate artery infarction of VPL and VPM produces delayed contralateral central neuropathic pain (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome).

open.q: Name the syndrome and specific thalamic nuclei damaged when a stroke causes delayed severe contralateral burning pain and allodynia.
accept: Dejerine-Roussy (central post-stroke thalamic pain) syndrome; Ventral Posterolateral (VPL) and Ventral Posteromedial (VPM) nuclei
Dejerine-Roussy syndrome; VPL and VPM thalamic nuclei

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m2) who recently started high-dose isotretinoin for severe acne presents with daily throbbing headaches worse when lying flat, transient visual obscurations when bending over, and pulsatile tinnitus. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling (papilledema), brain MRI/MRV is normal without mass or venous thrombosis, and lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 36 cm H2O with normal CSF protein and cell count. What is the diagnosis and first-line pharmacotherapy?
options: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri); treated with weight loss and acetazolamide
Bacterial meningitis; treated with ceftriaxone
Subarachnoid hemorrhage; treated with nimodipine
Normal pressure hydrocephalus; treated with levodopa
questions.explain: Elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) + papilledema + normal MRI/CSF in an obese young woman on vitamin A analogs is classic for idiopathic intracranial hypertension, managed with acetazolamide to lower CSF production.

open.q: State the diagnosis and the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to decrease CSF production in an obese young woman with headaches, papilledema, normal MRI, and opening ICP of 36 cm H2O.
accept: Pseudotumor cerebri / idiopathic intracranial hypertension; acetazolamide

questions.q: A 57-year-old man is brought in by his wife because over the past year he has become socially inappropriate—making crude sexual jokes to strangers, shoplifting small items, eating compulsively, and showing complete lack of empathy—while his memory and visuospatial skills remain intact. Neurological exam reveals grasp and palmomental reflexes, and MRI shows focal atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal poles. Which cortical region accounts for his behavioral disinhibition?
options: Orbitofrontal / ventromedial prefrontal cortex (behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia)
Left posterior superior temporal gyrus
Right primary visual cortex
Left postcentral gyrus
questions.explain: Orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal degeneration (behavioral variant FTD / Pick's disease) causes early personality change, social disinhibition, and primitive frontal release reflexes before memory loss.

open.q: Which prefrontal cortical region is damaged when a patient develops early social disinhibition, impulsivity, and primitive grasp/snout reflexes with preserved memory?

questions.q: A 65-year-old man develops sudden-onset weakness of his RIGHT leg and foot, urinary incontinence, and abulia (lack of initiative/spontaneity), while his face and right arm strength remain completely normal. Which cerebral artery is occluded?
options: Left Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) supplying the medial frontal lobe and paracentral lobule
Left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)
Right Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)
Basilar artery
questions.explain: ACA infarction affects the medial motor/sensory homunculus (contralateral leg/foot weakness and sensory loss) and medial frontal micturition/motivational centers (urinary incontinence and abulia).

open.q: Identify the occluded cerebral artery in a patient presenting with contralateral lower-limb weakness/sensory loss, urinary incontinence, and abulia with spared face and arm strength.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man recovers from herpes simplex virus-1 encephalitis that damaged both anterior medial temporal lobes. Post-recovery, he exhibits remarkable placidity without fear or anger, puts inedible objects such as erasers and pencils into his mouth, makes inappropriate sexual advances, and fails to recognize familiar objects visually until he touches them. Which bilateral structure was destroyed?
options: Bilateral amygdalae (Kluver-Bucy syndrome)
Bilateral caudate nuclei
Bilateral red nuclei
Bilateral lateral geniculate nuclei
questions.explain: Bilateral amygdaloid destruction (commonly post-HSV-1 encephalitis) produces Kluver-Bucy syndrome (placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, visual agnosia).

open.q: Name the syndrome and bilaterally damaged limbic structure in a post-HSV encephalitis patient exhibiting placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia.

questions.q: A 33-year-old man sustains an acute epidural hematoma from a middle meningeal artery tear. In the emergency department, his blood pressure rises to 198/112 mmHg, his heart rate drops to 44 bpm, and his breathing becomes irregular. Why is his heart rate dropping despite severe intracranial emergency?
options: Raised ICP causes sympathetic hypertension, followed by baroreflex vagal bradycardia
Raised ICP directly stimulates the SA node, causing tachycardia and hypertension
Low ICP activates vagal withdrawal, causing hypertension and bradycardia
Raised ICP suppresses sympathetic output, causing hypotension and tachycardia
questions.explain: Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) is an ominous sign of critically elevated ICP and impending brainstem herniation. Critically raised ICP compromises brainstem perfusion and triggers intense sympathetic vasoconstriction to preserve cerebral perfusion pressure. The resulting hypertension activates arterial baroreceptors, increasing vagal output and slowing the heart; irregular respirations complete Cushing's triad.

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanism producing bradycardia during Cushing's triad in a patient with critically elevated intracranial pressure.
accept: Brainstem ischemia triggers massive sympathetic vasoconstriction to raise systemic arterial pressure (preserving cerebral perfusion), which activates arterial baroreceptors and drives vagal parasympathetic slowing of heart rate
Baroreceptor-mediated vagal reflex bradycardia secondary to ischemia-induced sympathetic hypertension

questions.q: A 63-year-old right-handed man presents with inability to write (agraphia), inability to calculate simple subtraction (acalculia), inability to name which finger the examiner touches (finger agnosia), and confusion between left and right, while speech fluency and motor strength are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: Left (dominant) angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule (Gerstmann syndrome)
Right posterior parietal cortex
Left occipital pole
Right supplementary motor area
questions.explain: Agraphia + acalculia + finger agnosia + left-right disorientation localizes precisely to the dominant (left) angular gyrus (Gerstmann syndrome).

open.q: Name the syndrome and specific dominant-hemisphere gyrus damaged when a patient presents with agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman recovers from bilateral occipital-temporal strokes affecting the ventral visual 'what' stream. Although she has 20/20 visual acuity and can accurately copy a drawing of a key, she cannot name or recognize the key by looking at it—yet as soon as the key is placed in her hand, she immediately says 'It's a key!' What is this condition?
options: Associative visual agnosia (bilateral inferior occipitotemporal cortex lesion)
Cortical blindness (Anton syndrome)
Astereognosis
Wernicke's aphasia
questions.explain: Intact visual perception/copying + inability to recognize objects visually + immediate recognition by touch or sound defines associative visual agnosia.

open.q: What condition is present when a patient with intact visual acuity cannot recognize familiar objects by sight, yet recognizes them immediately upon touching them?

questions.q: A 68-year-old man suffers a large left internal carotid artery stroke involving the entire perisylvian language network (Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and arcuate fasciculus). On examination, he produces only a single recurring syllable ('tan, tan'), cannot follow any spoken or written commands, and cannot repeat single words. What type of aphasia does he have?
options: Global aphasia
Conduction aphasia
Transcortical motor aphasia
Anomic aphasia
questions.explain: Global aphasia combines non-fluent speech + impaired comprehension + impaired repetition due to extensive destruction of both anterior and posterior perisylvian language areas.

open.q: Identify the aphasia type characterized by non-fluent speech, impaired comprehension, and impaired repetition resulting from extensive left perisylvian infarction.

questions.q: A 24-year-old medical student volunteers for a sleep physiology study. Ninety minutes after falling asleep, her EEG shifts abruptly from high-amplitude <4 Hz waves to low-voltage, high-frequency sawtooth/beta-like waves, rapid conjugate eye movements appear on EOG, and submental chin EMG becomes completely flat. If awakened at this exact moment, what will she most likely report?
options: A vivid, detailed narrative dream (REM sleep)
Complete inability to recall any mental imagery (Stage N3 slow-wave sleep)
Having been wide awake solving calculus problems
An episode of sleepwalking around the laboratory
questions.explain: Desynchronized EEG + rapid eye movements + chin EMG atonia occurring ~90 minutes after sleep onset marks the first REM sleep period of the night, strongly associated with vivid dreaming.

open.q: Which sleep stage is identified by low-voltage desynchronized EEG, rapid eye movements, and flat chin EMG ~90 minutes after sleep onset?

questions.q: Which EEG rhythm, at 8 to 13 Hz, is seen over the occipital region in a relaxed adult with the eyes closed?
options: Beta
Alpha
Theta
Delta
questions.explain: The alpha rhythm is the dominant posterior rhythm of relaxed wakefulness. It disappears when the eyes open or the person concentrates.

open.q: Which EEG rhythm, at 8 to 13 Hz, is seen over the occipital region in a relaxed adult with the eyes closed?

questions.q: Which EEG rhythm, at 13 to 30 Hz, is typical of an alert adult with the eyes open and the mind active?
options: Alpha
Theta
Delta
Beta
questions.explain: Beta activity is fast and low in amplitude and is most prominent over the frontal regions during mental activity.

open.q: Which EEG rhythm, at 13 to 30 Hz, is typical of an alert adult with the eyes open and the mind active?

questions.q: Which EEG wave, below 4 Hz and high in amplitude, is the main rhythm of deep slow-wave sleep?
options: Delta
Theta
Alpha
Gamma
questions.explain: Delta waves dominate stage N3 sleep. In an awake adult they point to a diffuse cortical lesion or encephalopathy.

open.q: Which EEG wave, less than 4 Hz and high in amplitude, is the main rhythm of deep slow-wave sleep?

questions.q: What underlies the replacement of the alpha rhythm by low-voltage fast activity when a person opens the eyes?
options: Synchronisation of cortical neurons
Onset of slow-wave sleep
Desynchronised cortical activity
Cortical inhibition
questions.explain: Sensory input and arousal through the reticular activating system make cortical neurons fire out of step. The EEG becomes fast and low in amplitude.

open.q: What process underlies the replacement of the alpha rhythm by low-voltage fast activity when a person opens the eyes?

questions.q: Which structure acts as the main pacemaker for the synchronised rhythms recorded on the EEG?
options: Hypothalamus
Cerebellum
Thalamus
Hippocampus
questions.explain: Thalamocortical circuits generate and synchronise the rhythmic cortical activity recorded at the scalp.

open.q: Which structure acts as the main pacemaker for the synchronised rhythms recorded on the EEG?

questions.q: Sleep spindles and K complexes are characteristic of which stage of sleep?
options: Stage N2
Stage N1
Stage N3
REM sleep
questions.explain: Stage N2 is light sleep and occupies about half of the night. Spindles are 12 to 14 Hz bursts, and K complexes are sharp biphasic waves.

open.q: Sleep spindles and K complexes are characteristic of which stage of sleep?

questions.q: In which stage of sleep do sleepwalking and night terrors mainly occur?
options: REM sleep
Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
questions.explain: These parasomnias arise from deep slow-wave sleep, mostly in children. The person is hard to wake and has no memory of the episode.

open.q: In which stage of sleep do sleepwalking and night terrors mainly occur?

questions.q: Which EEG pattern is seen during REM sleep?
options: High-voltage delta waves
Fast low-amplitude waves
Frequent sleep spindles
Regular alpha waves
questions.explain: The REM EEG is desynchronised and looks like the waking EEG, although the person is asleep.

open.q: What type of EEG activity is seen during REM sleep?

questions.q: Why is REM sleep also called paradoxical sleep?
options: Breathing stops during dreams
Delta waves appear despite dreaming
Muscle tone rises in deep sleep
EEG resembles waking in a sleeper
questions.explain: The brain looks active on EEG while the person is deeply asleep and the muscles are paralysed. This is the paradox.

open.q: Why is REM sleep also called paradoxical sleep?
accept: Awake pattern in a sleeping person
Active brain with a paralysed body

questions.q: Which change in skeletal muscle tone occurs during REM sleep?
options: Atonia of most skeletal muscles
Increased tone in antigravity muscles
Unchanged tone throughout the body
Rigidity of the limb muscles
questions.explain: Brain stem inhibition of spinal motor neurons causes atonia, which stops dreams from being acted out. The diaphragm and extraocular muscles are spared.

open.q: What happens to skeletal muscle tone during REM sleep?

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is mainly responsible for initiating REM sleep?
options: Noradrenaline
Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Histamine
questions.explain: Cholinergic neurons of the pontine tegmentum fire strongly in REM sleep. Noradrenergic and serotonergic neurons fall silent.

open.q: Which neurotransmitter is mainly responsible for initiating REM sleep?

questions.q: REM-off neurons, which fall silent during REM sleep, are found in which nucleus?
options: Pedunculopontine nucleus
Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Locus coeruleus
Lateral geniculate nucleus
questions.explain: The locus coeruleus (noradrenergic) and the raphe nuclei (serotonergic) are active in waking and silent in REM sleep. The pedunculopontine nucleus is REM-on.

open.q: Which pontine noradrenergic nucleus contains REM-off neurons that fall silent during REM sleep?

questions.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus acts as the master circadian clock?
options: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Supraoptic nucleus
Paraventricular nucleus
Arcuate nucleus
questions.explain: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies above the optic chiasm and sets a rhythm of about 24 hours. It is reset daily by light.

open.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus acts as the master circadian clock?

questions.q: Which pineal hormone rises in darkness and promotes sleep?
options: Cortisol
Serotonin
Oxytocin
Melatonin
questions.explain: Melatonin is made from serotonin in the pineal gland. Secretion is driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus and suppressed by light.

open.q: Which pineal hormone rises in darkness and promotes sleep?

questions.q: Which retinal cells project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and entrain the circadian rhythm to light?
options: Rod photoreceptors of the peripheral retina
Melanopsin-containing ganglion cells
Cone photoreceptors of the fovea
Bipolar cells of the retina
questions.explain: Intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells containing melanopsin send signals through the retinohypothalamic tract. They do not contribute to image formation.

open.q: Which retinal cells containing melanopsin project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus?

questions.q: Damage to which of these structures most commonly causes coma when it involves both sides?
options: Cerebellar vermis and flocculus
Caudate nucleus and putamen
Midbrain reticular formation
Anterior commissure and fornix
questions.explain: The reticular activating system in the upper brain stem keeps the cortex awake. Bilateral damage there, or widespread cortical damage, causes coma.

open.q: Damage to which brain stem structure most commonly causes coma?

questions.q: A patient has no purposeful response to commands but has sleep-wake cycles, spontaneous breathing and roving eye movements. What is the most likely condition?
options: Brain death
Locked-in syndrome
Coma
Vegetative state
questions.explain: In the vegetative state the brain stem and arousal systems work but the cortex is severely damaged, so wakefulness is present without awareness. In coma the eyes stay closed with no sleep-wake cycles.

open.q: A patient has no purposeful response to commands but has sleep-wake cycles, spontaneous breathing and roving eye movements. What is the most likely condition?

questions.q: Broca area, responsible for speech production, lies in which gyrus of the dominant hemisphere?
options: Inferior frontal gyrus
Superior temporal gyrus
Angular gyrus
Precentral gyrus
questions.explain: Broca area covers Brodmann areas 44 and 45 and plans the motor programme for speech. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.

open.q: In which gyrus of the dominant hemisphere does Broca area lie?

questions.q: Which area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere is responsible for comprehension of speech?
options: Broca area
Wernicke area
Primary auditory cortex
Angular gyrus
questions.explain: Wernicke area (Brodmann area 22) interprets the meaning of spoken and written language. The primary auditory cortex only receives the sound.

open.q: Which area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere is responsible for comprehension of speech?

questions.q: After a left middle cerebral artery stroke, a man speaks fluently but with meaningless words and cannot understand commands. What type of aphasia does he have?
options: Broca aphasia
Conduction aphasia
Wernicke aphasia
Global aphasia
questions.explain: Damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus gives fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension. In Broca aphasia comprehension is preserved and speech is non-fluent.

open.q: After a left middle cerebral artery stroke, a man speaks fluently but with meaningless words and cannot understand commands. What type of aphasia does he have?

questions.q: A patient has fluent speech and good comprehension but cannot repeat phrases. Which structure is most likely damaged?
options: Arcuate fasciculus
Inferior frontal gyrus
Posterior temporal lobe
Primary motor cortex
questions.explain: The arcuate fasciculus links Wernicke and Broca areas. Its loss causes conduction aphasia, with intact comprehension and speech but poor repetition.

open.q: A patient has fluent speech and good comprehension but cannot repeat phrases. Which structure is most likely damaged?
accept: Pathway between Wernicke and Broca areas
Fibre bundle linking the speech areas

questions.q: Which cerebral hemisphere is dominant for language in most right-handed people?
options: Right hemisphere
Both hemispheres equally
Neither hemisphere
Left hemisphere
questions.explain: The left hemisphere is dominant for language in nearly all right-handers and in most left-handers.

open.q: Which cerebral hemisphere is dominant for language in most right-handed people?

questions.q: In a split-brain patient, an object shown only in the left visual field cannot be named. Why?
options: The right visual cortex is destroyed by surgery
The left optic nerve is cut during surgery
The image cannot reach the language hemisphere
Broca area is disconnected from the motor cortex
questions.explain: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere. With the corpus callosum cut, the information cannot cross to the left hemisphere, which controls speech.

open.q: In a split-brain patient, an object shown only in the left visual field cannot be named. Why?
accept: Right hemisphere cannot signal the left hemisphere

questions.q: Which structure is most important for consolidating new declarative memories?
options: Cerebellum
Hippocampus
Amygdala
Caudate nucleus
questions.explain: The hippocampus in the medial temporal lobe is needed to turn short-term memories into long-term declarative memories. The amygdala adds emotional colouring.

open.q: Which structure is most important for consolidating new declarative memories?

questions.q: After bilateral medial temporal lobe removal, a patient cannot form new declarative memories but remembers events from before the surgery. What is this called?
options: Anterograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia
Dementia
Dissociative fugue state
questions.explain: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories. In retrograde amnesia old memories are lost instead.

open.q: After bilateral medial temporal lobe removal, a patient cannot form new declarative memories but remembers events from before the surgery. What is this called?

questions.q: Which type of memory, such as riding a bicycle, is largely independent of the hippocampus?
options: Episodic
Semantic
Working
Procedural
questions.explain: Procedural (implicit) memory for skills depends on the basal ganglia and cerebellum. Patients with hippocampal damage can still learn new motor skills.

open.q: Which type of memory, such as riding a bicycle, is largely independent of the hippocampus?

questions.q: Which synaptic mechanism is thought to underlie learning and memory in the hippocampus?
options: Synaptic fatigue
Long-term potentiation
Neuronal apoptosis
Myelin remodelling
questions.explain: Repeated strong stimulation causes a lasting increase in synaptic strength, which stores information.

open.q: Which synaptic mechanism is thought to underlie learning and memory in the hippocampus?

questions.q: Which receptor, blocked by magnesium at resting potential, is essential for induction of long-term potentiation?
options: AMPA receptor
GABA-A receptor
NMDA receptor
Nicotinic receptor
questions.explain: Strong depolarisation removes the magnesium block of the NMDA receptor. Calcium then enters and starts the changes that strengthen the synapse.

open.q: Which receptor, blocked by magnesium at resting potential, is essential for induction of long-term potentiation?
accept: Ionotropic glutamate receptor with voltage-dependent magnesium block

questions.q: A 7-year-old child has sudden 10 second staring spells with unresponsiveness. The EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What type of seizure is this?
options: Absence seizure
Complex partial seizure
Myoclonic seizure
Tonic-clonic seizure
questions.explain: Typical absence seizures begin in childhood and show 3 Hz spike-and-wave on the EEG. There is no aura and no postictal confusion.

open.q: A 7-year-old child has sudden 10 second staring spells with unresponsiveness. The EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What type of seizure is this?

questions.q: After a road accident with damage to the prefrontal cortex, which change is most likely?
options: Loss of speech comprehension
Inability to form new memories
Loss of vision in the opposite field
Poor judgement and personality change
questions.explain: The prefrontal cortex handles planning, judgement and social behaviour. Damage causes disinhibition, apathy and personality change, as in the case of Phineas Gage.

open.q: After a road accident with damage to the prefrontal cortex, which change is most likely?
